messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elena was a 43-year-old chef who had spent over two decades building a career around her hands. She could chop a mountain of onions without looking, balance a dozen pans at once, and plate a dish with the precision of a surgeon. That last metaphor had never occurred to her before the infection. It started as a small nick on her index finger while she was breaking down a case of salmon. She rinsed it, wrapped it in a kitchen towel, and kept working. Within three days the finger was hot and swollen, but Elena shrugged it off—chefs didn't stop for cuts. By the fifth day she was on the floor of her walk-in cooler, shaking with fever, unable to call out because her throat had closed. A line cook found her just before she lost consciousness. The next thing she remembered was the ICU: the ventilator tube scraping her throat, the beeping of machines, a nurse’s face swimming in and out of focus. The sepsis had nearly killed her; she spent two weeks sedated and another month learning to walk again. The doctors told her she was lucky. Elena did not feel lucky.

What she felt, in the months after she returned home, was a terrible distance from everything she had once known. Her partner, Marcus, would bring her tea and she would nod, but the warmth of the mug felt like a photograph of warmth—seen, not felt. She had come to believe that the part of her that used to feel joy or excitement or even simple contentment had been cut out along with the dead tissue from her finger. When Marcus suggested they go to a friend’s birthday dinner, Elena felt a flash of panic that surprised her. The thought of sitting in a restaurant, of laughter and clinking glasses, felt obscene. She told him she was tired. She was always tired, but she also feared that if she let herself feel happy even for a moment, something terrible would yank it away. Better to stay flat. Better to stay safe.

The memory itself arrived without warning, not as a story she could tell but as a full-body possession. She would be standing over a stockpot and suddenly the smell of antiseptic would swamp the scent of simmering bones. The ventilator tube—the suffocating pressure of it, the way it made her gag—would come back as a sensation in her throat, so real that she would clutch her neck and gasp. Her body reacted before her mind understood: her heart would hammer, her palms would sweat, and she would find herself crouched behind the prep table, shaking, as if the danger were still in the room. She began to see her body as a traitor, a machine that kept triggering alarms when there was no fire. Worse, she was certain that the illness had left her permanently fragile. Every twinge in her chest was the start of another sepsis, every ache a sign that her body was giving out again. She could not relax even at home—she would lie on the sofa scanning her own pulse, waiting for the floor to tilt.

Sleep became the enemy. Every time Elena closed her eyes, the ICU came back in full sensory clarity: the cold plastic of the bed rail, the hum of the ventilator, the weight of a hand lying lifeless on the sheet. She learned to stay up until two or three in the morning, scrolling through kitchen equipment catalogues or reorganizing her spice rack, anything to postpone the moment when the memory would swallow her whole. She was exhausted, but exhaustion felt safer than surrender. And worst of all was the grief. When she remembered the event, it was not the fear that hit her hardest—it was the loss she had never allowed herself to acknowledge. She had almost died. She had come within hours of never seeing Marcus again, never tasting her own food again. That grief rose up like a wave and she could not breathe through it. Sometimes she found herself weeping while peeling carrots, with no idea why she had started.

Work, which had once been her refuge, became a minefield. The kitchen at the restaurant was full of triggers: the smell of raw fish, the gleam of a knife blade, the sight of her own scarred finger. She started delegating prep work to her sous chef, then she started leaving early when the dinner rush got loud. Her hands trembled over the stove. Her boss noticed and told her to take more time off, but Elena knew that staying home would be worse—she would just sit in the dark, avoiding Marcus’s concerned glances, avoiding the phone calls from friends, avoiding the living room where they used to watch movies and laugh. She was not living; she was surviving on the smallest possible footprint of contact with the world.

What finally brought Elena to seek help was a night when Marcus found her sitting on the bathroom floor at 3 a.m., staring at her hands. She had been trying to tell him that she felt nothing, that she was empty, but the words came out wrong. He said, “You’re not here.” And she realized he was right. She was not here. She was somewhere inside the memory, still fighting, still waiting for the beep of the heart monitor to stop. She agreed to see a therapist because she could not imagine another year like this, but also because she was terrified that the therapy itself would force her to feel something she could not survive. What she was most afraid of was that the grief would not stop—that if she let herself cry about what happened, she would never stop crying. What she was most hoping for, though she could barely admit it, was that somewhere beneath the numbness there was still a person who could taste a perfect sauce and smile.
